Architecture Diagram

This application is a single web application that serves a photo gallery and stores its image content in Azure Blob Storage. The browser communicates with MVC actions, which use the Azure Storage SDK directly.

Data Storage & External Services

The application persists images in one Azure Blob Storage container named webappstoragedotnet-imagecontainer. The configured development default uses the local Azure Storage emulator; a deployed environment requires a storage-account connection string. No relational database, cache, message broker, or other external service is configured.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Uses a single MVC controller to implement gallery listing, upload, and deletion.
  • Accesses Azure Blob Storage directly through its SDK rather than through a separate repository or service layer.
  • Stores images as blobs and exposes their URIs to the browser.

DTOs & Contracts

No custom request or response DTOs are present. The upload action consumes ASP.NET’s multipart request file collection; the index action passes a list of blob Uri values to the view. The application uses the Azure SDK’s BlobItem and BlobClient types internally. No OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL contract was found. JSON serialization is not part of the application’s exposed action contract.

Communication Patterns

Browser-to-application communication is synchronous HTTP using MVC form submissions and redirects. The controller invokes the Azure Blob Storage SDK for listing, upload, and deletion; SDK storage operations use Azure service requests. There is no message broker, service discovery, gateway aggregation, configured retry/circuit breaker policy, or client-side load balancing in the application. The configured connection string chooses the storage endpoint. No application-level authentication, authorization, or TLS policy is configured in the project; transport security can be supplied by the hosting environment.

Core Business Workflows

The application lets users browse a photo gallery backed by blob storage, upload image files, and delete individual or all stored blobs. No additional domain services or multi-service business process is present.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
Gallery BlobWebApp-Storage-DotNet / Photo GalleryAn uploaded object displayed as a gallery imageBelongs to the configured blob container
Blob ContainerAzure Blob Storage / Image StorageHolds the gallery’s stored objectsContains gallery blobs

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
WebApp-Storage-DotNetPhoto GalleryGallery view and blob operationsAzure Blob Storage
Azure Blob StorageImage StorageBlob objects and containerNone identified

There are no cross-service domain exchanges; the web application directly invokes the storage service.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the Gallery

  1. The browser requests the default Home/Index page.
  2. The controller creates the container if it does not exist and lists the container’s block blobs.
  3. The controller converts blob names to URIs and passes the list to the Razor view.
  4. The view renders links and thumbnails for each URI.

Workflow 2: Upload Images

  1. The user selects files and submits a multipart form to Home/UploadAsync.
  2. The controller iterates over the submitted files and generates a unique blob name using the current tick count, a GUID, and the original extension.
  3. The file is uploaded to the configured container.
  4. The controller redirects the browser to the gallery.

Workflow 3: Delete Images

The browser posts a selected blob URI to Home/DeleteImage; the controller extracts its file name, deletes that blob if it exists, and redirects to the gallery. Home/DeleteAll iterates through block blobs in the container, deletes them, and redirects.

Cross-Service Data Flows

The web application calls Azure Blob Storage directly to create the container, enumerate blobs, upload files, and delete blobs. The gallery view receives blob URIs for display. There is no aggregation across multiple services or fallback behavior for a downstream service outage; storage exceptions are rendered using the error view.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User as "Gallery User" participant Web as "Photo Gallery" participant Storage as "Azure Blob Storage" User->>Web: Open gallery Web->>Storage: Ensure container and list blobs Storage-->>Web: Blob list Web-->>User: Render image gallery User->>Web: Submit selected image files Web->>Storage: Upload blobs with generated names Storage-->>Web: Upload results Web-->>User: Redirect to refreshed gallery User->>Web: Request image deletion Web->>Storage: Delete selected blob Storage-->>Web: Delete result Web-->>User: Redirect to refreshed gallery

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Only blobs whose storage type is Block are included in gallery listing and bulk deletion.
  • New blob names are generated using a timestamp and GUID while retaining the selected file extension.
  • Individual deletion extracts a file name from the submitted URI and uses DeleteIfExistsAsync; bulk deletion processes each block blob.
  • No application-level authentication, authorization, input validation, upload-type allowlist, or audit trail is implemented.
  • Storage exceptions are caught and rendered in the error view; no compensating action or business transaction is present.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The application targets .NET Framework 4.8 and uses older MVC, Razor, JSON, jQuery, and Bootstrap package versions. The legacy non-SDK project format and Visual Studio Web Application targets also constrain cross-platform builds and modernization to newer .NET versions.

Notable Observations

  • packages.config lists 34 package declarations; all 34 are shown in the diagram. No test-scoped dependencies or package lock file were found.
  • Azure Blob Storage is the only application-specific persistence dependency.
  • Legacy jQuery 1.10.2, Bootstrap 3.0.0, and Newtonsoft.Json 6.0.8 are notable modernization and maintenance risks.
